page.title: When to use tinyactors
page.description: When tinyactors fits a program and when it does not, what a crash keeps, and how it compares with Temporal, Durable Objects, Rivet and XState.

hero.headline: Use it when your program owns the process
hero.lede: tinyactors is a library on your own event loop: your program owns the process, the store and every effect. Each actor runs an SCXML chart, where an Erlang or Akka actor runs any code.

section.heading: Use it for many long-lived stateful entities
section.p: tinyactors fits a program whose entities wait days for their next event, such as orders or chat sessions:

item.text: An idle actor is saved to your store and loaded on its next event. Two million actors ran with at most 1000 in memory.
A test answers the chart's sends and moves its clock, so a payment that retries every 30 seconds runs in milliseconds.
One C core runs the same chart in Node.js, Python, a browser and C, and every binding runs the same tests.
A chart sends an event for each effect, and an I/O processor in your code performs it.

section.heading: Look elsewhere for free code or failover
section.p: Some needs belong to another tool, or to work your program does itself:

item.text: A tinyactors actor runs an SCXML chart: states, events and transitions, with expressions in JavaScript or Python. An Erlang or Akka actor runs whatever code you give it.
Placement and failover are your program's work, as deployment is. It runs a host in each process and writes the transport that carries sends between them (other systems).
The project is under active development, and its README says breaking changes are made frequently.

section.heading: A crash keeps what you saved
section.p: Actors live in your process's memory, so a crash or a restart stops every one of them. What comes back is what your program saved:

claim.statement: A snapshot brings every actor back
claim.p: Host.restore runs a snapshot in this process or another, with each actor's variables, queued events and pending timers.
claim.source: Snapshots, "Copy every actor into one buffer"

claim.statement: A blob wakes only with its host
claim.p: A hibernated actor's blob carries its host's random identity. A new host refuses it, and a host restored from that host's snapshot accepts it.
claim.source: Hibernation, "Wake each blob where it was made"

claim.statement: What came after the snapshot needs replaying
claim.p: A restored host starts at the snapshot's time and accepts blobs its actors hibernated since. Your program replays the other inputs from a journal it keeps.
claim.source: Snapshots, "Replay the inputs that came after"

claim.p: The core does no I/O. tinyactors saves blobs through the store you give it, and takes a snapshot when your program asks.
claim.source: Snapshots, "Keep your backups in your database"

section.heading: Your charts are W3C SCXML documents
section.p: A chart is a document in SCXML, a W3C standard. Your code meets tinyactors at events: inputs go in, and effects come out to your handlers.

claim.p: The core passes all 191 automatic tests of the W3C's SCXML suite, and every binding runs the same suite.
You may use, change and ship tinyactors, keeping its copyright and permission notice.

claim.statement: Snapshots and blobs are tinyactors' own
claim.p: A snapshot restores only on a build with the same memory layout. Keep the data that must last in your database.

section.heading: tinyactors runs where your program runs
section.p: Each tool below keeps actor or workflow state somewhere. tinyactors keeps it in your process, and saves it to the store you give it.

claim.statement: Temporal runs a service beside your program
claim.p: A Temporal Service is the Temporal Server with its persistence stores. Self-hosted, it runs on Docker, Kubernetes or by hand.
A tinyactors host is an object your program creates, so a test needs no Docker and no cluster.
Cloudflare describes a Durable Object as a Worker that combines compute with storage, placed near its first request.
A tinyactors actor runs in any process that runs your program: a server or a browser tab.

claim.statement: Rivet places its actors for you
claim.p: Rivet describes its actors as durable processes in your backend, placed by Rivet Cloud or your own control plane.
A tinyactors actor stays in the host that spawned it, and your program decides where each host runs.
XState's README says it is inspired by the SCXML specification. tinyactors runs SCXML documents themselves, the same chart in every language.
